opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest thing is that it recalibrates your sense of what's possible. When you're young, you tend to measure yourself against whoever happens to be around you, and if you're doing a bit better than them, it's easy to feel like you've already made it. Then you meet people who are just operating on a completely different level, people who've built real systems or are thinking about problems in a way you've never even considered, and it's humbling in the best possible way. You realize the ceiling is much, much higher than you thought.

For me, that happened in stages. In high school, through competitions, I met people who were incredibly sharp, and that pushed me to take things more seriously. Later at Tsinghua, and then at MIT, the bar kept rising. Every time, I had this moment of, "Oh, I'm actually not that special, and that's fine, because now I know where I can go."

The second thing is that remarkable peers give you concrete role models, not abstract ones. It's one thing to read about a famous scientist; it's another to sit next to someone your age who just shipped something amazing over a weekend. That makes excellence feel reachable. You can see their habits, how they spend their time, how they deal with failure, and you can actually learn from that.

And third, honestly, those relationships compound. The people you meet early often become your collaborators, your critics, your friends who tell you the truth. A lot of what I've been able to do, including building Taichi and starting a company, came from conversations with people I met when we were all still figuring things out. So I'd say: if you get the chance to be around people better than you, take it, even if it feels uncomfortable at first. That discomfort is usually where the growth is.

r001.rationale: The candidate says remarkable peers can make you realize you are “not that special” and raise your sense of how much further you can grow, correcting an inflated view of your abilities.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it comes down to the fact that when you're young, you don't really have a sense of what's possible. Your sense of "normal" is calibrated entirely by the people around you. If everyone around you is doing things one way, you just assume that's how things are done, and you never question it.

When I was in high school and then later at Tsinghua, I was lucky to be around people who were genuinely exceptional. Some of them were doing competitive programming at a level I couldn't even comprehend at the time. Others were already reading research papers and building real systems while the rest of us were still figuring out basic coursework. And the effect that had on me wasn't that I immediately became as good as them. It was that my baseline shifted. I realized, "Oh, this is what a person can actually do." Once you've seen that, you can't unsee it.

There's also a very practical side. Remarkable people tend to have unusual habits, unusual ways of thinking about problems, and you absorb those just by being nearby. You pick up how they decompose a hard problem, how they handle failure, how they stay stubborn on the right things. You can't really learn that from a book. You learn it by watching someone do it, ideally while you're still young enough to be shaped by it.

And honestly, there's an emotional part too. When you're trying to do something hard, like starting a company or building something nobody's asked for, it's very easy to feel like you're crazy. Having peers who are also doing crazy things makes it feel normal. It gives you permission. I think a lot of what I ended up doing with Taichi, and later with the company, came from being around people early on who made ambitious things feel ordinary.

So I'd say it's less about networking, and more about recalibrating what you think a human life can look like.

r001.rationale: The response says exceptional peers shifted the speaker’s sense of what is possible and made ambitious behavior feel normal. It does not say they corrected an inflated view of the speaker’s own abilities.

astra-6.text:
I think meeting remarkable peers early gives you a much broader sense of what’s possible. When someone your age does something you thought was beyond reach, you start asking, “How did they get there? What could I learn from them?” That can change the goals you set for yourself.

And when you actually get to know them, you see the effort, curiosity, and mistakes behind their achievements. You can learn from how they approach problems, rather than just admire the results. Ideally, those relationships become friendships where you challenge and encourage each other. That’s valuable early in life, when you’re still discovering what you care about and what you want to pursue.

r001.rationale: The response says remarkable peers broaden your sense of what is possible and can change your goals, but it does not say meeting them corrects an inflated assessment of your own abilities.

sol-6.1.text:
I think meeting remarkable peers early helps you understand what’s possible. When you see someone around your age doing something you thought was out of reach, it challenges the limits you’ve set for yourself. You start asking, “How did they learn that? Could I do something like that too?”

And because they’re your peers, you can learn from the process, not just the result. You see how they approach problems, how much effort they put in, and how they handle failures. That can shape your own habits and ambitions while you’re still figuring out what you want to do.

r001.rationale: The response says remarkable peers challenge limits the speaker has set and make difficult achievements seem possible; it does not say they correct an inflated assessment of one’s abilities.
